panels.figure_caption: Loss of spine biomechanics. Anteroposterior spine radiograph in a 7-year-old child showed vertebral malsegmentation, that is, hemivertebrae and butterfly vertebrae (T6-11), respectively (arrow) (a) Three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction computed tomography (CT) scan of the spine and the thoracic cage in a 9-year-old boy with autosomal recessive Robinow syndrome presented with rigid spine movements (loss of the physiological spine biomechanics). He showed massive spondylothoracic malsegmentation associated with rib fusions and bifid ribs seen adjacent to the malsegmented spine segments. Strikingly, spina bifida occulta at the level of T3 and T10 (arrowheads) associated with a posterior malsegmented bar runs along T5-T8 on top of bilateral failure of segmentation. In addition to multilevel ribs fusions (right side, fusions of ribs 4 and 5, followed by fusions of 6, 7, and 8 ribs, respectively [arrow]). On the left side, fusions of ribs 6 and 7 followed by fusions of ribs 10 and 11 causing effectively the development of bifid rib (b).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Anterior 3D CT in 6-year-old boy with autosomal dominant Robinow syndrome shows T2/3 malsegmentation, matching vertebral segmentation defect synonym for hemivertebrae finding; article states this is most notable feature in all patients. b: Posterior 3D CT confirms fusion of T2/3 without rib fusions in same Robinow syndrome patient, matching congenital vertebral segmentation defect.

panels.figure_caption: Thoracic kyphosis. Three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction computed tomography (CT) scan in a 6-year-old boy with autosomal dominant Robinow syndrome who presented with thoracic kyphosis showed malsegmentation of T2/3 (anterior view-arrow). The 3D reconstruction CT scan (posterior view) confirmed the malsegmentation along the T2/3 and not associated with rib fusions.
in_text_mentions: 4. Spine: In all patients, vertebral malsegmentation was the most notable features, not associated with rib fusions and or unsegmented bars. A 6-year-old boy with ADRS presented with thoracic kyphosis. Three-dimensional reconstruction CT scan, anteriorly (a) showed malsegmentation along T2/3 and posterior view (b) clearly showed the fusion of T2/3 without rib fusions (Figure 5a and b).

He had practically no rotations of the forearm [Figure 1c]. The humerus was normal. Other features observed were hypertelorism and broad and prominent forehead. Disease-focused Robinow Syndrome article title plus specific captioned mesomelic manifestation supports Robinow attribution. b: Panel b is 3D CT of upper limbs in 5-year-old girl explicitly captioned as autosomal recessive Robinow syndrome with marked mesomelic dysplasia, Madelung deformity and small hands with camptodactyly.

panels.figure_caption: Radioulnar dislocation and severe retardation of the fine motor skills. Anteroposterior radiograph of the upper limb in a 7-year-old child. Note the marked mesomelia and the superior and inferior radioulnar dislocations (arrow head) with Madelung’s-like deformity associated with camptodactyly of the fourth and fifth fingers, respectively (a). Three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction computed tomography (CT) scan of the upper limbs in a 5-year-old girl with autosomal recessive Robinow syndrome showed bilateral radioulnar superior and inferior dislocation (Madelung’s deformity—arrow head) with marked dysplastic process over the epi metaphyseal components, small hands with bilateral camptodactyly of the fourth and fifth fingers (arrow). All patients with autosomal recessive Robinow syndrome presented with marked limitations in pronation and supinations because of mesomelic dysplasia secondary to Madelung’s deformity (b).

Note the marked mesomelia and the superior and inferior radioulnar dislocations (arrow head) with Madelung’s-like deformity associated with camptodactyly of the fourth and fifth fingers, respectively (a). Three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction computed tomography (CT) scan of the upper limbs in a 5-year-old girl with autosomal recessive Robinow syndrome showed bilateral radioulnar superior and inferior dislocation (Madelung’s deformity—arrow head) with marked dysplastic process over the epi metaphyseal components, small hands with bilateral camptodactyly of the fourth and fifth fingers (arrow). All patients with autosomal recessive Robinow syndrome presented with marked limitations in pronation and supinations because of mesomelic dysplasia secondary to Madelung’s deformity (b).

Normal skeletal maturity was assessed through hand wrist graphs (Figs 4B and C) which exhibited clinodactyly of fifth finger. The patient was referred to the department of Pediatrics for further evaluation where she was identified as a case of Robinow syndrome. Patient underwent full body survey. plate_findings.evidence: Dorsal spine X-ray film showing scoliosis, block vertebrae and hemivertebrae

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Dorsal spine radiograph from a Robinow syndrome case (article title and in-text confirm Case 2) showing scoliosis, block vertebrae and hemivertebrae, which are classic vertebral manifestations of the disease. b: Skull radiograph from the same Robinow syndrome case showing crowded teeth, a recognized dental manifestation of the disease; the finding is not covered by the provided vocabulary so it is placed in proposed_findings.
panels.attribution_text: Suresh. Robinow syndrome.. Indian journal of orthopaedics 2008. doi:10.4103/0019-5413.43399. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Case 2 (a) Dorsal spine X-ray film showing scoliosis, block vertebrae and hemivertebrae. (b) Skull X-ray film showing crowded teeth
in_text_mentions: The skeletal features in this patient were strikingly similar except that the scoliosis was of much severe degree [Figure 2a]. He also had the typical forearm deformity and costovertebral segmentation defects. This patient underwent functional endoscopic sinus surgery for antrochoanal polyp. His teeth were crowded [Figure 2b] and had gingival hypertrophy. His ears as in the previous case were low set, and the pinna was deformed.

panels.rationale: Single anteroposterior radiograph of both hands and forearms of a 5-year-old boy explicitly stated to have autosomal dominant Robinow syndrome. The image visibly shows the hand and forearm skeleton with caption-documented skeletal findings (rectangular first metacarpals, multiple pseudoepiphyses, clinodactyly) specific to Robinow syndrome; the figure's stated point is absence of Madelung deformity/radioulnar dislocation. Disease attribution is direct from the caption and article title. No vocabulary key exactly matches pseudoepiphyses/clinodactyly/rectangular metacarpals, so these are listed as proposed findings; brachydactyly is included as the closest vocabulary match for the digital/ray abnormalities visible on the hand radiograph. [raw subtype: autosomal dominant]

Journal of investigative medicine high impact case reports 2020. doi:10.1177/2324709620911771. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 6.
panels.figure_caption: Neither Madelung’s deformity nor radioulnar dislocation. Anteroposterior radiograph of the forearms in a 5-year-old boy with Robinow syndrome, autosomal dominant type, showed normal development of the radioulnar with normal pronation and supination. No camptodactyly, though rectangular first metacarpals, multiple pseudoepiphyses, and clinodactyly, were noted.
in_text_mentions: 5. Upper limbs: No mesomelic dysplasia has been elicited in these patients. Radiographs showed normal development of the radioulnar with normal pronation and supination. Anteroposterior radiograph of the forearms in a 5-year-old boy with ADRS showed normal development of the radioulnar with normal pronation and supination. No camptodactyly, though rectangular first metacarpals, multiple pseudoepiphyses, and clinodactyly, were noted (Figure 6; refer to Tables 1 and 2).
